title: Admission control + backpressure hooks for Dedicated tiers (burst limits, overload mode, throttling)
creator: Aisha Bello
description:
Context
Dedicated tiers (Standard / Performance / Premium) require enforceable behavior when customer load exceeds provisioned capacity or tier burst policy. Today we rely on “best effort” scheduler behavior + autoscaling lag, which results in unpredictable latency and sporadic throughput dips during load spikes. This issue adds tier-aware admission control and overload backpressure hooks aligned to the tier semantics from ADR-0128.

Goals
- Ensure Dedicated deployments degrade predictably under overload (throttle/shed quickly vs building queue/latency).
- Enforce tier burst ceilings in a measurable, auditable way (via metrics and logs), consistent across control plane + gateway + runtime.
- Make SRE alerting and Support triage unambiguous: we should be able to distinguish “SLO breach” vs “expected throttling due to customer exceeding tier policy”.

Non-goals
- Rewriting the provisioning pipeline (out of scope for this phase).
- Per-customer bespoke kernel tuning.
- Building a full customer-facing console redesign (DES-144 covers minimal surfacing).

Proposed design (implementation sketch)
1) Tier policy config surface (control plane → gateway/runtime)
- Add a small, versioned tier policy object to Dedicated deployment config (source of truth: control plane).
- Fields (initial):
  - tier_name: standard|performance|premium
  - burst_multiplier (float): allowed short-term throughput above sustained target
  - burst_window_s (int): sliding window for burst accounting
  - overload_queue_max_ms (int): maximum queueing time before shed
  - max_inflight_requests (int): hard cap to prevent unbounded concurrency
- Gate behind feature flag: dedicated_admission_control_v1

2) Admission control at the gateway (primary enforcement)
- Maintain a per-deployment token-bucket / leaky-bucket style limiter keyed by deployment_id (Dedicated only).
- Input signal for “budget” should be tier target (control plane) with burst allowance; NOT measured instantaneous throughput (avoid feedback loop).
- Enforcement actions:
  - Soft throttle: return 429 with Retry-After when inflight cap or budget exceeded.
  - Hard shed: return 503 when queueing time exceeds overload_queue_max_ms OR when runtime is in overload_mode.
- Streaming specifics:
  - Admission decision should happen prior to sending the request to runtime (before prefill).
  - For long-lived streaming requests, do NOT terminate mid-stream in v1; the mechanism is “deny new work”, not “kill existing work”.

3) Overload mode hook in runtime (secondary enforcement + observability)
- Expose a runtime signal “overload_mode” to gateway based on:
  - scheduler queue depth and queueing time
  - GPU saturation / decode backlog
- When overload_mode=true, gateway should prioritize shedding new requests earlier (avoid waiting to time out).

4) Metrics / logging (must be SLO-friendly)
- Counters:
  - dedicated_admission_denied_total{deployment_id,tier,reason} reason ∈ {burst_exceeded,inflight_cap,overload_mode,queue_max_ms}
  - dedicated_admission_allowed_total{deployment_id,tier}
- Gauges:
  - dedicated_inflight_requests{deployment_id}
  - dedicated_runtime_overload_mode{deployment_id} (0/1)
- Histograms:
  - dedicated_gateway_queue_ms{deployment_id} (if applicable)
- Logs:
  - Structured log line on deny with reason, retry_after_ms, request_id, deployment_id, tier.

Acceptance criteria
- Tier policy config is plumbed from control plane to gateway for Dedicated deployments (behind FF), and validated (missing/invalid config fails closed with clear error).
- Under synthetic overload, gateway returns 429/503 consistently with correct reason labels, rather than allowing unbounded queue growth.
- SRE dashboards can separate:
  - low throughput due to throttle (expected) vs
  - low throughput due to platform regression (actionable incident)
- Load test shows:
  - queueing time bounded (no runaway p99)
  - stable behavior during autoscaling lag (throttle instead of timeouts)
- Documentation snippet for Support / CS: what customers will see (HTTP status + headers) and how to interpret throttling.

Open questions
- Should we prefer req/sec limiter or output tokens/sec limiter at the gateway?
  - Current plan: limiter expressed in “request admissions per second” and “max inflight requests” for v1, to avoid needing token predictions.
  - Follow-up: move to token-based budgets once request token estimation is standardized (ties into throughput measurement standard).
- Should 429 be used for all throttling reasons, or split 429 (policy) vs 503 (platform overload)?
  - Current plan: 429 for burst/inflight policy; 503 for overload_mode/queue_max_ms.

Implementation plan
- Phase 1 (this issue):
  - Gateway: add per-deployment limiter + deny responses + metrics/logs.
  - Runtime: expose overload_mode signal + queueing time metric consumption.
  - Wiring: tier policy config + feature flag.
- Phase 2 (follow-up issue):
  - Token-aware budgeting (prefill token estimate + decode tokens) and tighter coupling to throughput SLI.

References
- ADR-0128 Tiering model and burst policy (source of semantics)
- PR-18457 Admission control policy scaffold for Dedicated tiers (initial code)
- ENG-2194 Instrument Dedicated throughput SLI metrics (needed for dashboards + future token-aware control)
- ENG-2210 Shape catalog + tier mapping in control plane (source of tier policy defaults)

Risks / mitigations
- Risk: deployment_id cardinality in metrics too high.
  - Mitigation: keep deployment_id metrics internal only; add aggregation by tier/region; sampling for logs.
- Risk: throttling changes customer experience.
  - Mitigation: ship behind feature flag, pilot with 1–2 beta Dedicated customers; publish “what to expect” doc; CS playbook update.
- Risk: incorrect limiter defaults cause underutilization.
  - Mitigation: conservative defaults + override support; monitor “allowed vs denied” rates; quick rollback via FF.
comments: 2025-01-24 (Keiko Yamamoto): Drafted v1 design: gateway-first admission control + runtime overload_mode signal. Keeping v1 request/inflight-based; token-based budgets later once we have reliable token estimation at the edge. Will align response semantics with Support (429 policy vs 503 overload).

2025-01-27 (Noah Patel): +1 to avoid a feedback loop using measured tokens/sec as the limiter input. Use static tier target + burst window. For runtime overload_mode, please ensure it’s derived from queueing time / backlog and not raw GPU util (util is noisy and model-dependent).

2025-01-28 (Sofia Ivanova): Scheduler can export queue_depth and queue_wait_ms; we can compute overload_mode as queue_wait_ms > threshold for N consecutive samples. Recommend threshold based on tier latency guardrail (e.g., 250–500ms queue). Let’s avoid per-request “kill” for streaming in v1; deny new work is safer.

2025-01-30 (Aisha Bello): From SLO governance POV, we need a clean label for “expected throttling” so it doesn’t page as a throughput breach. Please add dedicated_admission_denied_total with reason. Also include a runbook note: if throttling rate spikes but throughput SLI is low, that’s customer load exceeding tier, not an incident.

2025-02-03 (Rafael Mendes): Ensure oncall can quickly answer: did we throttle or did we fall below guarantee without throttling? Add a single dashboard panel “Denied % by reason” and “Overload mode over time” for each deployment. Also need paging hygiene: do NOT page on denial rate alone; page on SLO burn + (denial rate low).

2025-02-06 (Keiko Yamamoto): Implemented limiter skeleton behind dedicated_admission_control_v1; opening PR building on PR-18457. Next: wire tier policy from control plane config (blocked on ENG-2210 fields) and add Retry-After header for 429. Need review on exact header units (ms vs seconds).

2025-02-09 (Mina Haddad): Heads up: tier policy needs to be consistent with routing policies (burst across regions is out of scope, but we should document that burst is per deployment_id, not global account). I can help verify config semantics once ENG-2210 lands.

2025-02-11 (Keiko Yamamoto): Ran synthetic overload test on a staging Dedicated deployment: without limiter we see queue_wait_ms spike > 3s and request timeouts; with limiter enabled we cap inflight at 64 and return 429 before timeouts start. Remaining gap: add 503 path when runtime overload_mode is true; waiting on runtime metric hook from Sofia.
